query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy, the absence of Co lowers the activation barrier for grain boundary (GB) mediated nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ partial dislocations, so that under identical deformation conditions the alloy will exhibit an earlier onset of plasticity (i.e., stress drops and stacking fault formation) compared to the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy in a solidified, solid-solution state with well‐characterized GBs (e.g., Σ configurations) similar to those used in prior simulation studies.
generation.intervention: Perform atomistic simulations combining GB-resolved molecular dynamics with high-strain-rate ballistic impact simulations; concurrently, conduct a controlled comparison with the equiatomic Cantor alloy under the same GB configurations.
generation.conditions: Simulations (and/or experiments) under controlled temperature (e.g., room temperature at 300 K versus elevated temperature around 1000 K) and strain rates (10^7 to 10^9 s⁻¹) using bicrystal setups with defined GB misorientations (e.g., Σ3, Σ9, Σ19) in an NPT ensemble.
generation.structural_mediator: The GB structure, which acts as an efficient site for nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ partial dislocations, mediating the onset of stacking fault formation and plastic flow under tensile deformation.
generation.mechanism: Due to the absence of Co, the local chemical heterogeneity and lattice distortion at GBs is altered, reducing the energy barrier for GB-mediated dislocation nucleation. This leads to earlier nucleation of partial dislocations (and hence stacking faults) at lower applied strains/stresses. Temperature and strain rate further modulate this effect by altering thermal activation and mechanical loading conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic alloy baseline, the Co-free alloy will show a lower threshold strain and stress for dislocation nucleation (evidenced by an earlier stress drop and increase in stacking fault fraction). This difference is expected to be observable across the tested strain rate range and will become more pronounced at elevated temperatures due to enhanced thermal activation.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi Cantor alloy where previous simulations indicate that GB-mediated dislocation nucleation occurs at higher applied strains and stresses.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to systems where a well-defined GB structure is present and in the strain rate range of 10^7 to 10^9 s⁻¹ at temperatures from 300 K up to approximately 1000 K. It is specific to tensile deformation in simulation or experimental bicrystal setups.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences in nucleation thresholds and stress drops between the Co-free and equiatomic alloys are uncertain and may depend on the particular GB misorientation and simulation parameters. Calibration with experiments may be necessary to establish effect sizes.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of atomistic molecular dynamics simulations (supported by complementary micro-scale tests if feasible) on both the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy and the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, using identical bicrystal models with controlled GB misorientations. Apply uniaxial tensile loading at multiple strain rates (10^7, 10^8, and 10^9 s⁻¹) and temperatures (300 K and 1000 K) and monitor the strain and stress levels at which dislocation nucleation events occur.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to capture the onset of stress drops
Fraction of stacking fault atoms as a function of strain
Dislocation density and nucleation timing via DXA or similar analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free alloy does not exhibit a consistently lower dislocation nucleation threshold (i.e., lower critical strain/stress, earlier stress drop, or increased stacking fault formation) than the equiatomic alloy under the same test conditions, or if the modulation by temperature and strain rate is absent or opposite to prediction, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Here, the PTM algorithm was used to identify the local structural environment around each atom and reveal GB regions and stacking faults that form during deformation. Figure 5 depicts results for the bicrystal system with a Σ9 [110] STGB, where Fig. 5a is a schematic illustrating the intersection of a {111} plane with this GB. Figure 5b–d shows respectively projected views normal to this {111} plane at nominal tensile strains ϵ=5.0%,5.4% and 5.5%, where the GB region is labeled in blue, FCC atoms in green, and HCP ones, indicative of stacking faults, in red. A 1/6 ⟨112⟩ partial dislocation line, identified by DXA and labeled in black, was observed to nucleate from the GB and propagate into the bulk crystal leaving behind a stacking fault, and that the nucleation of this partial dislocation corresponded to the stress drop observed for this bicrystal system (refer to Fig. 4b). While the Cantor alloy has been the subject of numerous studies in recent years, most of these have been mainly focused on the effects of element compositions away from the equiatomic one, stacking fault energies,, and lattice distortions. The role of GBs in the mechanical deformation of HEA alloys remains poorly understood. Tensile stress-strain diagrams for Cantor alloy bicrystals with [110] and [111] loading axes show that GBs facilitate the nucleation of partial dislocations, which with further deformation grow in the bulk crystal leaving behind stacking faults. This is in agreement with recent experimental findings demonstrating that GBs act as nucleation sites for mechanical nanotwins,. The bicrystals with a [111] loading axis were found to require more mechanical energy to nucleate dislocations from GBs compared to systems with a [110] loading axis. As shown in Figs. 5 and 6, nucleation of 1/6⟨112⟩ dislocations in the bicrystal systems occurred at lower strain values compared to their single crystal counterparts. Results of the simulation are given in the Supplementary Materials (see fig. S6 for comparison), which show that the stress-strain curves at each strain rate at different temperatures are similar, suggesting that the failure mechanisms of the two HEAs at the high strain rates do not change with increasing temperature, although the HEAs are softened at elevated temperatures.

reading.lever: Combine GB-resolved atomistic simulations with high-strain-rate ballistic impact simulations in a new Co-free alloy.
reading.why: This integrated simulation approach leverages proven techniques on related HEA systems to uncover the temperature and strain rate dependence of dislocation nucleation in the Co-free alloy.
